new_statements.rule_in_words: By contrast with adverbs, the citation form of a Libido noun (which is the accusative, as in other Highland East Cushitic languages) is stressed on its final syllable; the nominative is distinguished from it by a different stress placement, so stress shift carries case (cf. the Crass & Meyer 2007 volume snippet placing Libido with the HEC accent-marked nominative pattern, and König 2008 listing Libido and Hadiyya among languages encoding case by stress change). Adverbs are not final-stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Adverbs (not stressed on the final syllable, hence no accusative/nominative distinction); the nominative form of nouns bears stress elsewhere (position not visible in the snippet; in the sister language Hadiyya the citation-form prominence is penultimate per Tadesse Sibamo 2015:31).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation form of nouns (= accusative) at word level; stress is case-sensitive (accusative vs nominative), so the 'final' rule holds for the citation form only. The statement is inferred by the explicit contrast 'adverbs differ from nouns in that..'; the surrounding text (and any dedicated phonology note in the chapter's introduction) was not visible.
new_statements.identity_note: Libido = Marako/Maraqo/Mareqo (endonym Libixxiso), Glottolog libi1250, ISO liq, Mareko woreda south-east of Butajira. Sister of Hadiyya (hadi1240); Bender 1976 and Blench 2006 treat it as a Hadiyya dialect, Glottolog and Crass as a separate language. Crass 2017 describes Libido proper (his own fieldwork); the Hadiyya penultimate pitch accent statement (Tadesse Sibamo 2015) is NOT transferable — Crass's Libido sentence points to final stress in the noun citation form.

sources.citation: Mous, Maarten. 2021. The grammatical primacy of tone in Cushitic [Crossref title: The Typology of Tone and Cushitic]. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 62: 91-106. DOI 10.5842/62-0-898.
sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog high1285). Argues Cushitic 'pitch accent' languages are restricted tone languages in Hyman's typology whose tone is primarily grammatical; states that the Highland East Cushitic languages meet the criteria of stress languages (one accented syllable per word; accent placement distinguishes case, e.g. Kambaata, Alaaba absolutive vs nominative; Sidaama 'pitch accent (high tone)' on the penultimate mora) and reports Appleyard's (1991) proposal that HEC lost its tone. No Libido data.

tone.quote: A number of Cushitic languages obey the criteria of stress languages. [...] Among the Highland East Cushitic languages, K'abeena has stress on the ultimate or penultimate syllable depending on the status of the final vowel (whispered or fully voiced; Crass 2005). Alaaba has word-level stress [...]. In Kambaata, every word has one accented syllable (Treis 2008). Sidaama has pitch accent (high tone) on the penultimate mora which moves to the ultimate mora in morphology (Kawachi 2007: 63-71). [...] In terms of historical development of tone/accent systems, Appleyard (1991) has proposed that Highland East Cushitic lost its tone
